title: Valparaiso stuns Purdue: Buzzer-beating 3-pointer in 2OT sends Boilermakers to first 0-2 start since 1976 - CBS Sports
description: Purdue entered Friday's game against Valparaiso as a 19.5-point favorite
body:
Purdue entered Friday's game against Valparaiso as a 19.5-point favorite

        Another major upset in college basketball headlined on Friday night in West Lafayette, Indiana, when Valparaiso handed Purdue a stunning 83-80 loss in double overtime. With the game tied at 80 in the final seconds, Valpo guard Justus McNair knocked down a corner 3-pointer as time expired to hand Purdue its second loss of the season.Valpo sent the game to double overtime after Rakim Chaney knocked down a 3-pointer at the buzzer to tie the game at 70. The Boilermakers led by as many as 15 points in the first half.The Boilermakers were 19.5-point favorites against Valparaiso and are now 0-2 for the first time since the 1976-77 season. Purdue is the latest high-major team to suffer a stunning loss during the opening week of the season. On opening night, Oklahoma lost to East Texas A&M as a 28.5-point favorite.
Purdue was riding a 23-game home winning streak during November. The loss to Valpo marked the first loss against a Missouri Valley Conference opponent at Mackey Arena since 1978, when Purdue lost to a Larry Bird-led Indiana State team.
The Boilermakers are in the midst of a major transition after Braden Smith, Trey Kaufman-Renn and Fletcher Loyer departed the program. That trio was among the most experienced in the sport and helped Purdue reach the Elite Eight in their final season together. Kaufman-Renn, of course, is playing his sixth season of college basketball with Kansas after being granted a motion for a preliminary injunction against the NCAA.

body:
The wide receiver says he is 100% healthy and filing for NFL reinstatement, though a $13 million financial dispute remains
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 6, 2026
                            
                    at
    7:37 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            6 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Brandon Aiyuk returned to the team offices on Friday and has begun to take the necessary steps to file for reinstatement. Aiyuk recently hired agent Drew Rosenhaus to represent him, and the two addressed reporters ahead of their meeting with the team. The former Second Team All-Pro pass-catcher issued a short statement saying he's healthy and ready to go. "I'm feeling great, feeling healthy, been a long recovery process, long rehab process but I'm back to 100% and looking to get reinstated to the National Football League," Aiyuk said.
Aiyuk returning to Santa Clara was a big story on Friday. Well, big to everyone except 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan. He has since moved on from the Aiyuk drama and said he couldn't care less what happened during Friday's meeting. 
There are a few obstacles that Aiyuk will have to navigate before he can suit up again. Tom Pelissero of The Ringer reports that Aiyuk owes the 49ers about $13 million in bonus forfeiture. If you recall, the team signed Aiyuk to a four-year, $120 million extension in August of 2024, then voided about $27 million of salary guarantees in July the following year after he did not meet the requirements in his contract. Aiyuk was then placed on the reserve/left squad list. Pelissero reports that the NFL management council and the NFL Players Association are both working to find a resolution, although it may take some time. Additionally, the 49ers still own Aiyuk's rights. When he's reinstated by the league, the 49ers will have to trade or release him. San Francisco has failed to trade him in the past, meaning a release of his rights could be on the table after the $13 million problem is settled. 
This marks the beginning of the end to a strange saga that included a contract holdout, an injury, a desertion and a social media circus.What happened with Brandon Aiyuk?In 2023, Aiyuk had established himself as one of the best wide receivers in the NFL. He caught 75 passes for 1,342 yards and seven touchdowns as the 49ers made it all the way to Super Bowl LVIII. Aiyuk's 3.1 yards per route run that year ranked No. 3 behind Tyreek Hill and Nico Collins, and his 81.3% of receptions going for a first down or a touchdown ranked first in the NFL. Aiyuk joined Jerry Rice that year as the only players in franchise history to record seven 100-yard receiving games in a season. He was dynamic downfield, catching 14 of 20 passes thrown both outside the numbers and with 15+ air yards in 2023. It was the best rate (70%) of any player in the last four seasons (min. 20 targets), per CBS Sports Research. Aiyuk had one more year remaining on his rookie deal via the fifth-year option, but he wanted long-term security heading into 2024.  
Not long after the 49ers' Super Bowl loss to the Kansas City Chiefs, Aiyuk's girlfriend published an interesting TikTok. "This might have been the last day we touched foot on Levi's Stadium," she said, "because we might not be out here next year."However, 49ers general manager John Lynch said in March of 2024 that they were working on an extension with Aiyuk, and would not be trading him.
"Brandon's one that we think incredibly highly of, one of my favorite guys around our building," Lynch said, via the 49ers' official website. Things appeared to change as the offseason rolled on. Ahead of the 2024 NFL Draft, the 49ers began to explore a potential deal involving Aiyuk. The San Francisco Chronicle reported that the 49ers wanted a first-round pick for their top receiver. One NFL executive claimed, "they want too much." When the draft did roll around, the 49ers selected a wide receiver at No. 31 overall in Ricky Pearsall. Even after the addition of Pearsall, Lynch said on the "Pat McAfee Show," they were past trading Aiyuk or Deebo Samuel. 
"I'm doing everything in my power to keep our roster together," Lynch said. "That's my goal, and I don't question that. When you talk about guys like Brandon Aiyuk and Deebo, those are guys that we drafted, and we take a lot of pride in what they've become and who they've become. We couldn't be more proud of those guys. And so, during the course of drafts and offseasons, do conversations happen? Absolutely, they do. We're past that now. We're thrilled to add to that group."In June, the 49ers reported to mandatory minicamp. Aiyuk did not. He started talking about playing for other teams publicly, listing the Washington Commanders and Pittsburgh Steelers as potential landing spots."If not a Niners uniform, probably a Washington Commanders uniform," Aiyuk said during an appearance on "The Pivot" podcast. "If not a Washington Commanders uniform, probably Steelers uniform."
The next month, Aiyuk finally demanded a trade. Teams had reached out to the 49ers about Aiyuk, but were told San Francisco did not plan to trade him, per ESPN. Aiyuk did show up to training camp, but was "holding in" as he awaited a new contract. It got to the point where NFL Media reported that contract talks between Aiyuk and the 49ers had been stalled for quite some time, and it was more likely the star pass-catcher would be traded than find lucrative, long-term security in San Francisco.However, less than a month later, Aiyuk signed a four-year, $120 million extension with the 49ers. At $30 million per season, it tied the fifth-largest average annual value for a wide receiver contract at the time.
After sitting out offseason work and the preseason, Aiyuk started the 2024 campaign slowly. He failed to reach 50 yards receiving in each of his first four games before finally breaking out with 147 yards on eight catches in Week 5 against the Arizona Cardinals. He caught two passes for 37 yards the following week vs. the Seattle Seahawks, then tore his ACL in the Super Bowl rematch against the Chiefs in Week 7.Naturally, Aiyuk was forced to miss the remainder of the 2024 season, but questions started being raised about when he would return to the lineup in 2025. In November, The Athletic reported that the team had voided the $27 million of 2026 salary guarantees owed to Aiyuk in the summer after he failed to meet the obligations in his contract. The next month, Aiyuk was placed on the reserve/left team list. Shanahan said at the time that he hadn't seen Aiyuk "in forever" and that Aiyuk had been "extremely distant."Later that month, Aiyuk filmed himself driving 104 mph near the 49ers' stadium. The Santa Clara County District Attorney's Office issued a warrant for his arrest on a misdemeanor speeding charge -- which remains active to this day, by the way. 
Lynch publicly announced the 49ers would be taking calls on Aiyuk, but given that this was a receiver who seemingly quit on his team and his rehab, they didn't find a market. Still, San Francisco wasn't going to just release him. With Aiyuk still tied to the 49ers and unable to sign with another team, he began lashing out on social media. He called the 49ers "little-ass boys" during one rant posted to Instagram, and called the organization "stupid" for paying him."They mad 'cause they stupid," Aiyuk said. "They dumb. They mad that they paid me $50 million in eight months and then voided my guarantees for 2027. And I'm about to be on a new team in 2027. They mad at themselves for real. They acting like they mad at me, but they stupid ass mad at themselves."
Aiyuk started pretending as if he were close to signing with the Commanders and reuniting with his college quarterback in Jayden Daniels. In numerous videos, he donned Commanders gear and even claimed he bought a house in Ashburn -- where Washington's practice facility is located. However, Aiyuk had not applied for reinstatement and still had his rights owned by the 49ers. He missed the entire 2025 season, but has now shifted his focus. Aiyuk is finally playing ball and taking the necessary steps to finalize a divorce.

        This week in the NFL, the Cincinnati Bengals and Atlanta Falcons will do battle in Madrid, the Green Bay Packers will look to spoil Rob Gronkowski's Patriots Hall of Fame induction in New England, and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers attempt to make up ground in the NFC South against the surging Chicago Bears.Injuries are mounting across the league as we cross the halfway point of the 2026 season, and that includes at quarterback. Shedeur Sanders will make his first start of the season for the Cleveland Browns in place of Deshaun Watson as they take on the New Orleans Saints, Drew Lock replaces Sam Darnold in the lineup for the Seattle Seahawks, and Carson Wentz will try to make the most of his opportunity against the Buffalo Bills with Kyler Murray sidelined by a hamstring injury. Another notable injury storyline is with new Seahawks offensive guard Quenton Nelson. Just one week after trading a third-round pick and future fifth-round pick to the Indianapolis Colts for the eight-time Pro Bowl left guard, head coach Mike Macdonald told reporters that Nelson needs a minor knee procedure. NFL Media reports it's to clean out cartilage, as fragments have been causing an issue. Seattle says Nelson will avoid injured reserve right now, and is week-to-week. That means the Seahawks offensive line will likely revert to their old format, with Grey Zabel at left guard and Anthony Bradford at right guard.  Below, we will break down the final injury reports for all teams set to play on Sunday, beginning with our international game in Spain.

body:
Matches against Scotland and Ukraine feature six players with senior USMNT call-ups, led by 2024 Olympian Benjamin Cremaschi and eight European-based prospects

        The road to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics is underway as Steve Cherundolo's roster for games against Scotland and Ukraine has been named, and it's an experienced group of players. Six players on this roster have been called up to the United States men's national team, and four earned caps during the recent September/October international break, while Parma's Benjamin Cremaschi was a member of the 2024 Olympic squad and is eligible to still be involved in the 2028 edition of the tournament.Looking at the experience with eight players being based abroad and so many being on the fringes of the senior side, it shows just how deep the talent available to Cherundolo is for the Olympics during what is an exciting time for U.S. Soccer. "We're very excited to bring this talented and polished group of players together and begin our journey toward the 2028 Olympic Games," Cherundolo said. "We're eager to get to work, establish our identity and build a strong foundation for what lies ahead. Our first international matches will be a great opportunity to challenge ourselves, compete, and grow together as a team."They'll begin training for this camp alongside the senior team at the Arthur M. Blank National Training Center, similarly to how the United States women's national team set up their last camp. Not only does it showcase a synergy between the two sides, but it also provides both Cherundolo and Mauricio Pochettino with opportunities to oversee each squad, because when they're called next, considering how young the senior team is, too, there could be shifts between the two squads.It's an important camp as it's Cherundolo's first since taking over the U-23s, so we'll get our first look at how the United States youth stacks up under him against solid opponents from around the world. Given the experience that's available to him and how tight competition will be for the Olympics, as three overage players can go in the 23-man squad for the competition, everyone will need to be on their game immediately.

The Michigan-UConn heavyweight tilt features loaded backcourts and high-dollar transfer bigs.         You don't have to dig deep into the archives to hype-up Friday's game between No. 16 Michigan and No. 4 UConn in Boston. It's the rematch of the 2026 National Championship game. Dusty May and the always-quotable Yaxel Lendeborg aren't around anymore, but the star power isn't hard to find. Michigan believes it has the best backcourt in college basketball. Get this: UConn also believes it has the best backcourt in the sport.What more could you possibly want?Let's dive into the matchups to watch ahead of this big-boy brawl, starting with the projected starting lineups for each side:Michigan: G Elliot Cadeau, G Trey McKenney, G Roddy Gayle Jr., F JP Estrella and C Moustapha ThiamUConn: G Silas Demary Jr., G Braylon Mullins, G Jayden Ross, F Nik Khamenia and C Na'jai Hines
Where to watch UConn vs. Michigan liveDate: Friday, Nov. 6 | Time: 8 p.m. ETLocation: TD Garden -- BostonTV: TNT | Stream: Fubo (try for free)UConn vs. Michigan: Need to knowBest on best: Cadeau and Demary Jr. are both front-runners for the Bob Cousy Award, given to the best point guard in America. Cadeau is a wizard playmaker who mixes speed, power and creativity. In an ideal world, Cadeau would love to finish a game with 12 assists rather than 20 points, but new Michigan head coach Mike Boynton Jr. may need him to score more than ever before. That's easier said than done because Demary is an elite point-of-attack defender. Demary is all of 6-foot-5 who takes it personally if anyone works him for a bucket. The team with the best point guard play will win this game, but it's as close to a draw on paper.Portal bigs: UConn and Michigan had to replace a combined five NBA players who all played in the frontcourt. UConn spent big in the portal for Seton Hall transfer Na'jai Hines, who is a total freak. Michigan did the same with Cincinnati transfer Moustapha Thiam, who is expected to suit up in this one after missing the opener against Oakland with an illness. Bigs from the portal always take a little time to fully coalesce for their new teams, but UConn and Michigan don't have time to wait. Thiam and Hines need to be immediate difference-makers. 
Specifically, keep an eye on when UConn aggressively hard-hedges Michigan's ball screens. Hines can be a bit foul-prone when he's flying out to try and be disruptive. Those avoidable fouls drove Dan Hurley up a wall in the preseason and earned Hines plenty of time on the pine. Conversely, that coverage forces the ball out of Cadeau's hands and into Thiam's hands. The 7-foot-2 big fella has to make good decisions if Michigan wants to find good shots, but he's not a great passer (yet). Friday's test should be enlightening on both sides of the aisle.Preseason hints: Some over-index on preseason results. Others completely ignore them. The truth is likely more in the middle. In the preseason, UConn's defense looked way ahead of schedule. It put Purdue in clamps for long stretches. title: Kristaps Porziņģis stepping away from basketball to deal with health issues - CBS Sports
description: Porziņģis signed a two-year, $40 million deal with the Warriors in free agency this summer

Porziņģis signed a two-year, $40 million deal with the Warriors in free agency this summer

        Golden State Warriors big man Kristaps Porzingis announced Friday that he has "made the decision to prioritize my health and step away from the game I love" as he continues to deal with mysterious health issues. It's unclear when, or if, the 31-year-old Porziņģis will return to the court. Porziņģis has not played for the Warriors this season and reports earlier this week indicated that the team is withholding payments from him. He signed a two-year, $40 million deal with the Warriors in free agency this summer, but the second year of the deal only has a $3 million guarantee. Here is Porziņģis' full statement announcing his decision to step away from basketball: This season I was really looking forward to running it with this group, but as I ramped up, my body didn't respond the way I anticipated. I'm doing good, but I know what it takes, and I'm not where I want to be to perform at the level that I expect from myself. At this point, I've made the decision to prioritize my health and step away from the game I love. In this situation, I want to show the utmost respect for the Golden State Warriors and work with them to find a solution that makes sense. I'm thankful to my family and close ones for always being there. Much appreciation to all of you for the support. Porziņģis' career has been defined by health problems. He's played more than 57 games just three times since he was drafted No. 4 overall by the New York Knicks in 2015, and has dealt with significant injuries, including a torn ACL that cost him the entire 2018-19 season. In recent years, he's been limited by this mysterious illness that first became an issue in Boston during the 2024-25 season. Porziņģis started dealing with extreme fatigue and previously disclosed a diagnosis of postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, or POTS, which is characterized by rapid changes in heart rate when a person stands up and can lead to exhaustion and dizziness. "You know how people say, 'Oh, I'm so fatigued.' I've never used those words. I don't even like to speak in those terms, but I really was like that," Porziņģis said ahead of last season. "At that time, I could just lay on the couch and be a house cat."Porziņģis has been away from Warriors since SeptemberOver the last three seasons with the Celtics, Atlanta Hawks and Warriors, Porziņģis has only played 74 games. He has been away from the Warriors since late September and released a previous statement in mid-October shutting down rumors that he had been diagnosed with HIV or AIDS. At that point, the Warriors said Porziņģis would be out indefinitely. "Hello people, I'm working with doctors and experts to figure out how to be fully back to good health asap. Honestly, I'm getting better and better. I just have to stay patient, and I believe I'll be feeling great again soon," Porziņģis wrote. "It has definitely been frustrating dealing with some health stuff that you can't exactly pinpoint, on top of injuries throughout my career, so it has added up for sure, but we will get through it. Health is wealth. Thank you for all the support."
The Warriors hoped that Porziņģis would play a big role this season as a floor-spacing big, especially while Jimmy Butler (torn ACL) and Moses Moody (torn patellar tendon) remain sidelined. Instead, it seems more likely that he will never play for the franchise again. The Warriors have reportedly been trying to trade Porziņģis to use his $20 million cap figure, as explained by CBS Sports' Sam Quinn:While he would not have trade value as a player given his health status, he is essentially an expiring contract with only that small $3 million guarantee on the books for next season. That could potentially make him valuable to a team looking to move off of longer-term money, or the Warriors could entice another team into a trade using draft picks with Porziņģis serving only as the matching salary.
        
            
                Kristaps Porziņģis trade destinations: Three viable moves the Warriors could make to improve their roster
                
                    Sam Quinn                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
Despite Porziņģis' absence, the Warriors are off to a 6-3 start, putting them in seventh place in the extremely crowded Western Conference standings. Rookie big man Yaxel Lendeborg has stepped up in Porziņģis' place and provided a major boost on both ends of the floor. 
Through nine games, Lendeborg is averaging 21 points, 7.1 rebounds, 4.1 assists and 1.1 steals while shooting 49.2% from the field, including 39.6% from 3-point range.

title: Austin Simmons re-signs with Missouri: Tigers set for high expectations in 2027 with star QB returning - CBS Sports
description: With Simmons locked in, Missouri can now build a winning roster around him
body:
With Simmons locked in, Missouri can now build a winning roster around him
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 6, 2026
                            
                    at
    3:49 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Missouri has re-signed quarterback Austin Simmons for the 2027 season, sources confirmed to CBS Sports' Matt Zenitz. That gives the Tigers stability at the most important position on the field ahead of what could be a hectic offseason in the portal.After beginning the 2025 season as the starting quarterback at Ole Miss, Simmons lost his job to Trinidad Chambliss and transferred to Missouri in the offseason. Through eight games, Simmons has been an excellent fit and has the Tigers in the mix to reach the College Football Playoff.In his first season as a Tiger, Simmons has completed 63.3% of his passes for 1,952 yards, 16 touchdowns and two interceptions. It helps that Simmons has some of the best weapons in the SEC around him, as Cayden Lee and Donovan Olugbode are two of the top eight receivers in the conference.That trio has powered a passing offense that ranks fourth in the conference at 257.1 yards per game and 26th in EPA per dropback at 0.19. That aerial attack has been the biggest driver of Missouri's offense this season, and that should remain the case in 2027.
With Simmons guaranteed to remain in Columbia, that allows Missouri to start getting its ducks in a row for portal season. If the Tigers play their cards correctly, they could be a force next fall.Retaining weapons, replacing OLParticularly when it comes to the offensive side of the ball, Missouri should have the chance to retain most of its production. Getting the quarterback -- presumably the most expensive player -- locked in will help the Tigers get more cost certainty as it looks to re-sign other players.The top priorities will obviously be the wide receivers. Olugbode, who has 584 receiving yards and seven touchdowns, is only a sophomore. He will play at least one more college season, and Missouri needs to make sure he doesn't go anywhere.
Lee, on the other hand, leads the SEC in receiving yards and is a senior. He could chase his NFL dreams, but if he did want to return, there would likely be plenty of interest from other teams. Assuming uses that fifth year of eligibility, Lee might be expensive to re-sign, but it would be worth it based on what he's done with Simmons so far.The running back situation is similar. Jamal Roberts leads the SEC with 1,005 rushing yards and could make the jump to the NFL. Ahmad Hardy could do the same thing, but he may want to prove to NFL scouts that he's fully healed from the gunshot wound he suffered earlier this year. If Missouri could keep at least one of those players, it would be a great sign for the 2027 offense.Where the Tigers may need to do some work in the portal is along the offensive line. Missouri has several fifth-year seniors on the interior, and true senior Cayden Lee could be a 2027 NFL Draft pick at left tackle. If the Tigers lose all of those players, they'll have to go portaling, but at least inking Simmons to a new deal now will help the team develop a game plan for rebuilding the offensive line.
Perhaps most importantly, having a talented quarterback like Simmons makes Missouri an appealing spot for current players and prospective portal additions alike. While other teams are bound for a shake-up behind center, Missouri has a proven commodity at quarterback, and that's something Eli Drinkwitz will be able to pitch.

Saint Louis looks like a top-25 team and the firm A-10 favorite with Avila in the fold, but the College Sports Commission is currently blocking the reigning A-10 Player of the Year due to a roster-limit snafu.

                    at
    5:00 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Saint Louis star big man Robbie Avila, the reigning A-10 Player of the Year, will return to the Billikens for a fifth year of eligibility after Missouri judge Jason Sengheiser granted Avila a preliminary injunction, just a day before SLU's enormous non-conference tilt against rival Missouri. Avila was expected to suit up and make his 2026-27 debut for Josh Schertz's club, but it hit a late snag Friday. The College Sports Commission is blocking Avila's return to the floor because adding a 16th player to SLU's roster would violate the roster limits imposed by the injunctive relief settlement in House v. NCAA. Sengheiser's decision drew some eyebrow raises because the court order ruled that the NCAA was not allowed to enforce its roster limits to block Avila from returning to Saint Louis' already-filled, 15-man roster. "While we take no position on Mr. Avila's eligibility, we cannot effectuate a state court order that requires us to violate the explicit terms of a federal injunctive relief settlement by giving Saint Louis University an additional roster slot," the CSC released in a statement. "Mr. Avila may be eligible to play college basketball this season, but there is no roster slot available for him at Saint Louis University." There are currently over 50 fifth-year seniors who are eligible and 16 who are not at the high-major ranks, according to Sports Illustrated's Kevin Sweeney. Avila's representation is expected to fight the CSC's ruling. If eligible, Avila's return is a massive boon for Saint Louis and college basketball. Dubbed Milk Chamberlain, Larry Nerd, Cream Abdul-Jabbar or Rob Wave, Avila has become one of the most recognizable names in the game. 
He can hoop, too. Avila averaged 12.8 points and shot 41% from 3-point range on 4.6 attempts for a Saint Louis offense that ranked second in the country in effective field goal percentage last season. Saint Louis started 24-1 last year, en route to earning an at-large bid and the No. 9 seed in the NCAA Tournament. It bulldozed Georgia, 102-77, in the first round before falling short to eventual champion Michigan in the Round of 32. It was Saint Louis' first NCAA Tournament win since 2014.

With Avila back in the fold, Saint Louis would have four starters back and two more key rotation players who hooped in the Big Dance. Expectations are extremely high, especially after Saint Louis' brass held off high-major poachers from Schertz, who is the hottest name in the coaching carousel. Avila may need a bit of time to knock off the rust in the early-going, but its wheels up for Saint Louis' 2026-27 long-term outlook. The Billikins are now the only team in America to retain three high-volume 40% 3-point shooters. Avila, Trey Green and Ishan Sharma combined to deposit 233 3-pointers last year. Bombs away.
But it's more than just 3s that makes Saint Louis' offense so hard to guard. The threat of the aerial assault opens up the paint. When Avila was on the floor, Saint Louis shot a whopping 63% at the rim. The layup is the most efficient shot in basketball, and nearly half (45% to be exact) of Saint Louis' shots came at the rim thanks to Avila's ability to draw shot-blockers away from the basket and make reads as a passer.Saint Louis looks like a top-25 team if it all clicks and the firm A-10 favorite if Avila can play. We'll see what VCU says about that, though.

title: Is Drew Mestemaker really QB1? A troubling trend and lessons from Caleb Williams, Trevor Lawrence - CBS Sports
description: The Oklahoma State QB has become a popular QB1 choice, but his mistakes under pressure offer a warning – and some
body:
The Oklahoma State QB has become a popular QB1 choice, but his mistakes under pressure offer a warning – and some fascinating historical comparisons.
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 6, 2026
                            
                    at
    3:16 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            6 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Caleb Williams. Trevor Lawrence. Drew Mestemaker.Two former No. 1 overall picks and probably the hottest name in the 2027 NFL Draft all share a troubling distinction: Over the last decade-plus, only Williams and Lawrence had higher turnover-worthy-play rates under pressure in their final college seasons than Mestemaker has this year.But there's a catch. For Williams and Lawrence, those numbers were one-year blips after considerably better performances earlier in their college careers. For Mestemaker, the mistakes have followed him from North Texas to Oklahoma State … and they've gotten worse.
None of that means Mestemaker can't be the first quarterback selected in the 2027 NFL Draft. He's put himself squarely in the QB1 conversation, and for good reason. I have Miami's Darian Mensah just ahead of him, but there's a whole lot to like about Mestemaker's game. NFL teams will also have to answer an important question before investing a high first-round pick in him: What happens when defenses take away the easy throws and force him to make decisions under pressure?
Why Mestemaker belongs in the QB1 conversationThere's plenty to like about the Oklahoma State quarterback, who spent last season at North Texas. For starters, Mestemaker looks the part. He has a strong arm, throws with anticipation and will get through his reads. He's comfortable attacking all three levels, manipulates defenders with his eyes and has the patience to stand in the pocket, reset his feet and deliver fastballs into tight windows.
He has plenty of NFL-caliber throws on tape, especially on intermediate routes where he has to throw receivers open. It's easy to see why he's become a popular QB1 choice. But there are also stretches where he tries to do too much, and that's where the evaluation gets more complicated.The concern isn't just this seasonThrough Week 9 of 2026, Mestemaker has seven turnover-worthy plays on 54 dropbacks when he was pressured, according to PFF. That's a 13.0% rate, more than double the 5.8% median for the first-round quarterbacks in our historical comparison.
(A turnover-worthy play isn't just an interception. It can be a dangerous throw that a defender drops or another mistake that puts the football at risk. And while the number itself doesn't tell us everything, it helps identify decisions that might otherwise get lost in the box score.)Williams and Lawrence were the only first-rounders we looked at with higher rates in their final college seasons, but both had been considerably better the previous year. Williams went from 0.9% in 2022 to 15.3% in 2023, while Lawrence jumped from 1.6% in 2019 to 13.2% in 2020.Turnover-worthy play percentage and yards per attempt when pressuredQBSeasonTWP %YPACaleb Williams202315.3%6.8Trevor Lawrence202013.2%8.3Drew Mestemaker2026*13.0%4.5Jordan Love201910.9%2.8Sam Darnold201710.5%11.0Josh Allen20178.9%6.7Patrick Mahomes20168.5%9.4* 2026 season through Week 9. Source: PFFLook at Williams and Lawrence now. Both had bumpy starts to their NFL careers, and both are now two of the NFL's best quarterbacks. It's a pretty good reminder that A.) landing in the right situation is probably the most important factor in a young QB's development, and B.) troubling college numbers don't mean you're destined to fail at the next level.Mestemaker's struggles have followed him from North Texas to Oklahoma State. His turnover-worthy-play rate was 8.3% under pressure in 2025 before climbing to 13% so far this season. Over that span, he's put the ball in harm's way 13 times in 126 such situations. That's a 10.3% rate, and it's something NFL evaluators will have to consider.Of course, there's recent precedent for NFL teams looking past troubling numbers. I wrote last November about Ty Simpson's historically poor deep-ball accuracy, and we later learned just how much injuries had affected his play. The Rams still took him 13th overall in April, betting on everything else he did well.Here's what makes it even more interesting: Mestemaker has gotten much better at avoiding sacks, but he's also making more dangerous throws. Last season, he was sacked on roughly 21% of plays when pressured. That number is down to 11% this year, but while he's taking fewer sacks, he's also averaging a full yard less per pass attempt in those situations (5.6 to 4.5).The tape provides more clues. Mestemaker generally shows good footwork and accuracy when he has time, and he's capable of working beyond his first read. But there are also moments when he forces throws into coverage instead of taking the easier completion underneath, or when his accuracy suffers because he doesn't get his feet set.These aren't all necessarily mistakes caused by pressure, but they point to a similar concern: knowing when to challenge a defense and when to take what it's giving you.What Mahomes, Allen, Love and Darnold can tell usThe good news for Mestemaker is that other really talented quarterbacks have entered the NFL with concerns about their decision-making under pressure. A lot of them have gone on to be really good. Of course, not everyone develops the same way.Let's start with Patrick Mahomes. In his final season at Texas Tech, he had an 8.5% turnover-worthy-play rate when pressured, but he also averaged 9.4 yards per attempt and generated 14 big-time throws. Mestemaker, by comparison, has averaged just 4.5 YPA this season, with three big-time throws against seven turnover-worthy plays.Mahomes took risks, but he was also creating considerably more positive plays when things broke down. That's an important distinction because making dangerous throws is one thing; consistently making spectacular plays to offset those mistakes is another.Jordan Love offers a different lesson. His final season at Utah State was a mess compared with his outstanding 2018 campaign. He went from 32 touchdowns and six interceptions to 20 touchdowns and 17 picks, and his turnover-worthy-play rate under pressure jumped from 3.4% to 10.9%.Love averaged just 2.8 yards per attempt when pressured in 2019, even worse than Mestemaker this season. Green Bay still took him in the first round, betting on his physical talent and development. That patience paid off, a reminder that a concerning college season doesn't have to define a quarterback's NFL career.Then there's Josh Allen, who happens to be Mestemaker's favorite quarterback. Allen inspired him to wear No. 17, and Mestemaker has talked about relating to Allen's unconventional football journey.Allen's final college season wasn't nearly as productive as the one before. His passing yards fell from 3,203 to 1,812, his yards per attempt dropped from 8.6 to 6.7, and he completed just 56.3% of his passes. His turnover-worthy-play rate under pressure was 8.9%, yet Buffalo took him seventh overall because his physical tools were impossible to ignore.Allen developed into JOSH ALLEN. While Mestemaker's best ball is likely in front of him too, it's unfair to expect anyone to make the leap Allen made once he arrived in the league.Sam Darnold provides another example. His turnover-worthy-play rate under pressure was 10.5% in his final season at USC, but he also averaged 11.0 yards per attempt in those situations. Like Mahomes, he took chances, but he also made big plays when things broke down.The point isn't that Mestemaker will become the next Mahomes, Allen, Love or Darnold. It's that quarterbacks can overcome weaknesses, but the risks have to be weighed against what they do well and what they're capable of becoming.So where does that leave Mestemaker?I still like Mestemaker a lot and there's every reason to believe he could be the first quarterback taken in either this draft or in 2028, should he decide to stay in school another year. But the mistakes under pressure are real, and they're going to be a part of his evaluation.There's also time for him to get better, likely even a lot better. Remember, Mestemaker never started a varsity game at quarterback in high school; he was primarily a punter and safety before walking on at North Texas. He's already improved at avoiding sacks, and the next step is making smarter decisions when defenses disrupt his timing. Mestemaker has the talent to be the first quarterback selected whenever he enters the draft. But making NFL throws and making NFL decisions aren't the same thing. And how much he improves his decision-making under pressure could ultimately determine just how early he'll hear his name called.

title: Meet Texas Tech's Stephanie Okechukwu, the tallest women's college basketball player ever - CBS Sports
description: What we learned after the 7-foot-1 native of Nigeria made her college debut on Thursday
body:
What we learned after the 7-foot-1 native of Nigeria made her college debut on Thursday
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 6, 2026
                            
                    at
    3:46 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            5 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Texas Tech center Stephanie Okechukwu wrote her name into the record books on Thursday night when she won the opening tip in the Lady Raiders' 64-37 win over Charlotte, and officially became the tallest player to play in an NCAA Division I women's basketball game. Okechukwu, a 7-foot-1 center who hails from Nigeria, finished with six points, 10 rebounds and three blocks on 2 of 6 from the field in 21 minutes. Okechukwu is the first 7-footer to play NCAA women's basketball; the tallest player previously was 6-foot-11 Marvadene Anderson, who played nine games for Pittsburgh. Tallest players in NCAA women's basketball historyPlayerSchoolSeasonsHeightStephanie OkechukwuTexas Tech2026-Current7-1Marvadene AndersonPittsburgh2013-146-11Abbie BoutilierEastern Illinois2025-Current6-10Nicole DominguezMiddle Tennessee2025-Current6-10Suzy BendegueGeorgetown1999-20036-10Elena KravchenkoVirginia1997-20016-10Charlene BippsSan Diego1992-936-10Kathey MooreMemphis 1984-856-10Who is Stephanie Okechukwu?Okechukwu was born in Umunneochi, Nigeria. One of seven siblings, her hobbies outside of basketball include "swimming, reading and social media," and she speaks English, Igbo and Japanese. As a teenager, she left Nigeria for Japan, where she attended Fukuchiyama Seibi High School and gained significant basketball experience. Okechukwu, who has a 7-foot-4 wingspan and can dunk easily, signed with Texas Tech in January, but did not play in a game last season. In April, she participated in the Nigerian national team's training camp, though she was not a part of the country's final roster for the 2026 FIBA Women's World Cup. "Just a couple of years ago our program took a deep dive into the international recruiting space," Texas Tech associate coach and general manager Erik DeRoo said when Okechukwu signed with the program. "The international game has grown exponentially, which now provides prospects globally for us to recruit, and clearly with our current roster, it has already paid off. The relationships built over the last two years gave us an opportunity to recruit and eventually sign Stephanie."Okechukwu granted four years of eligibilityOkechukwu was initially granted two years of eligibility, but the NCAA reversed that decision on Wednesday, just over 24 hours before Texas Tech's first game. The program shared a video of Okechukwu learning the news, which brought her to tears. "I did my interview earlier and I started crying afterward. A positive cry, because obviously this story is really special to me," DeRoo said. "Right after I got done, I got a call from the NCAA that said that they granted you all four years of eligibility to play at Texas Tech. Which means you'd be here four years to get your degree.""Stop," Okechukwu said. "Are you serious? I literally think about this every day. Like it's, come on. Oh my god." "I don't think people know how much you want to get your degree," DeRoo said. "And I walked out, and I was like, man, we just changed the trajectory of her life knowing that we can get you a degree from Texas Tech."
Okechukwu, who is listed as a sophomore, will be able to play for Texas Tech through the 2029-30 season. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    What did we learn from Okechukwu's debut?Texas Tech coach Krista Gerlich told USA Today at Big 12 media day last month that Okechukwu has improved "tremendously" since she arrived in Lubbock in January. "It's been insane, actually. Just her getting in the weight room has been fantastic because she's really put on some good muscle and gotten a strong base," Gerlich said. "She's really understanding the terminology and she's understanding where we want to get her the basketball, how we can use her offensively and defensively."Still, Okechukwu has extremely limited high-level experience, and it was no surprise that her debut was full of ups and downs. Within the first 12 seconds, she won the opening tip, grabbed an offensive rebound, then missed the putback. Here's what we learned against Charlotte: 1. She's a major presence in the paintAs expected, Okechukwu's size is going to be an advantage in the paint on both ends of the floor. Charlotte didn't have anyone in their rotation taller than 6-foot-3, and while Texas Tech will play better and bigger opponents, none of them will be able to match Okechukwu's size. And all of them will feel her impact. On Charlotte's very first possession, Mariah Sain had a step on Ambrosia Cole, but pulled up when she saw Okechukwu waiting in the paint and missed a short jumper. 
Okechukwu blocked three shots and altered many others. In the 21 minutes Okechukwu was on the floor, Charlotte only took seven shots in the paint and made one, with three of the misses rejected by Okechukwu. All told, Charlotte managed just 11 points in the first half and 37 for the game on 14 of 55 (25.4%) from the field. 
Okechukwu was a presence on the glass, grabbing 10 rebounds -- four offensive and six defensive. If a rebound falls in her vicinity, opponents have little chance. Offensively, Okechukwu's shot is impossible to block, and opponents' desire to send multiple bodies at her before she's even made a catch can help open up shots for her teammates. Look here, as Sain sinks all the way into the restricted area even though Texas Tech's Tahys Da Silva is only one pass away. Sain can't recover in time, and Da Silva gets a wide-open 3. 
2. Okechukwu is still rawOkechukwu is still very raw, and has a lot of room to develop so that she can even more effectively use her size advantage. Her missed putback on the opening possession became a theme as she struggled with her touch around the basket and shot 2 of 6. She also traveled multiple times, had a blatant double dribble and was called for a three-second violation after getting stuck under the basket. 
She also needs to get better at establishing position in the post. Effort was not an issue in that regard, but Texas Tech could not get the ball to her down low in the halfcourt as often as you would expect.  3. Lack of mobility could be a problem against better teamsOkechukwu is not super mobile, and while Charlotte was unable to take advantage of that, better teams will. While Okechukwu's size is a major deterrent, she spends most of her time on defense camped out in the paint. Guards who can knock down pull-up jumpers out of the pick-and-roll or bigs who can step away from the rim -- even to the mid-range -- are going to cause her and Texas Tech problems. There were also a few occasions when Charlotte's bigs beat her down the floor in transition, though they couldn't capitalize. If future opponents are insistent on pushing the pace against the Lady Raiders, they could find success, especially after turnovers or missed shots.

        The 2026-27 MLB offseason is a bit more than a week old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. We've ranked the top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and built you a calendar of the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Friday's hot stove happenings.Skubal's market already hot
The market for two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, far and away the offseason's best free agent, is already hot, according to the New York Post. Skubal is expected to sign in November, before the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, though a deal is not imminent. Talks are underway, however, and his market is moving.Skubal is expected to sign a record contract at least in total value, and possibly in average annual value. Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million deal with the Dodgers is the largest pitching contract ever given out. Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander's matching $43.3 million salaries with the Mets years ago set the record for the average annual value for a pitcher.Several teams linked to SatoThe Dodgers, Mets, Padres, Phillies, and Yankees are among the teams linked to Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato, reports the New York Post. Unless MLB and the MLBPA unexpectedly avoid a lockout, Sato must sign before the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. Otherwise, he will return to the Hanshin Tigers for 2027.
We ranked Sato as the fourth-best free agent available this offseason, and the best available position player. He has significant power but also swing-and-miss and defensive concerns at third base, similar to Munetaka Murakami a year ago. Murakami slugged 35 home runs in only 127 games as a rookie this season, providing proof of concept for Sato.
        
            
                MLB free agency: Five international players to know for the 2026-27 offseason
                
                    Mike Axisa                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Nationals lock up Jacob Young
The Nationals have signed center fielder Jacob Young to a four-year extension, reports FanSided. The deal is worth $23 million and includes an $8 million club option for a fifth year. The extension buys out Young's three arbitration years and one free agent year, with a club option for a second free agent year. He's now under Washington's control through 2031.
Young, 27, has always been a superlative defender. He unlocked a new level on offense this season, particularly in the second half, when he hit .301 with a .385 on-base percentage. Young had been speculated as a trade candidate since last offseason, but the new extension locks him in as part of Washington's long-term core.

It's Week 9 of the NFL season, and for your Fantasy football squads, this is a pivotal week. With more teams on bye and major injuries to starting quarterbacks around the NFL, the fringe plays are now more mainstream and for good reason. Your stat/sit decisons have just gotten a lot more difficult and the matchups play an even more important role now than ever.  That's where Dave Richard's Week 9 matchup breakdown comes in. From defensive coverages and pass-rush pressure to backfield workloads and target distribution, we'll examine the factors that matter most to help you identify trustworthy starters, avoid potential disappointments and make the best possible lineup decisions.  Dave Richard's Week 9 rankings: Top 150 | QB | RB | WR | TE | K | DST  
                    
                Start 'em

Joe Fagnano has extensive college experience (starting at Maine for four years before transferring to UConn for two more years) and has proven to be a reliable, quick-game pocket quarterback. Asking him to be anything more than that might be problematic, even if his pass protection won't be too rough. Last year at UConn he connected with Skyler Bell on a ton of quick throws, but not necessarily all short throws, for huge numbers. My best guess is that the Ravens scheme up a slew of targets to Zay Flowers against the Jaguars' zone-heavy defense with the hope he breaks a couple of plays for big yardage. The Jaguars happen to rank bottom-five in both yards per attempt and average depth of throw allowed to receivers on throws under 2.5 seconds, but it's not like they've been crushed on quick passes -- Darius Cooper had a long touchdown against a coverage bust and Keenan Allen had a lot of quick-game volume to help push their numbers to decent totals. Tight ends like Foster Moreau and Mike Gesicki have had more success, so maybe that helps raise the outlook for Mark Andrews, who leads all tight ends and is second on the team with 21 targets on quick throws this season. It's probably not enough to call him anything more than a low-end streamer, though. That leaves Flowers as the only Ravens pass-catcher with decent Fantasy potential as a No. 2 receiver.   START: Trevor Lawrence, Bhayshul Tuten, Derrick Henry (No. 2 RB), Parker Washington, Zay Flowers (No. 2 WR), Jaguars DSTFLEX: Brenton Strange (PPR; high-end No. 2 TE)SIT: Joe Fagnano, Chris Rodriguez (bye-week RB unless Tuten is out), Mark Andrews (bye-week TE), Jakobi Meyers, Justice Hill (desperation PPR RB), Brian Thomas Jr., Rashod Bateman, Ravens DST

Kyle Pitts wasn't the problem last week -- his quarterback in the rain against a suffocating Buccaneers pass rush was. Pitts generally stuck to short-area routes as an easy option for Michael Penix Jr., though he was wide open on a deep corner that Penix overthrew. Penix otherwise melted down and threw four picks and three other shoulda-been picks. Pitts also didn't see any red-zone snaps until the final drive of the game when Penix was pressured and either misfired or had his ball batted down on three straight plays. Weather won't be a factor in Spain's stadium, and Cincinnati's pass rush has blitzed at the lowest rate this season with a league-average pass rush pressure rate. The Falcons haven't let Penix get sacked in either of their past two games, which is quite a feat given who they've played. This seems like a good spot for Penix, which means it's a good spot for Pitts to be trusted in what should be a high-scoring game.

Carolina's offensive problems last week started with an offensive line that let up pass-rush pressure on 52.2% of Bryce Young's dropbacks -- and six sacks. Denver's pass rush has only gotten more dangerous with Jonathon Cooper on the field and will be a big challenge for a Panthers O-line down to a third-string left guard and a rookie right tackle. That meant mediocre numbers for Carolina's wide receivers last week; a repeat is possible this week. Of the six wideouts to achieve at least 16 PPR points against Denver in 2026, five needed at least eight targets, three needed 12-plus. Just four touchdowns have been allowed to receivers, all of which came away from Pat Surtain, who will likely follow Tetairoa McMillan. Red-zone motion and crossing patterns have tripped up Denver on three of the TDs, but how many red-zone trips will the Panthers have? And for what it's worth, this Denver defense has yielded more touchdowns to tight ends than wide receivers on the year. Jalen Coker has more than five targets in just one of his past four games (and five max in each of his past two); getting him more involved might make some sense, but on the year Coker has just a 12.2% target per route run rate and a 1.04 yard per route run average when Young's been pressured. That's pretty rough; Tetairoa McMillan and Chuba Hubbard have much higher target rates when the heat's been on Young. I imagine they'll get more targets, especially McMillan on designed short throws, which has been the case lately. They've allowed a sack rate of at least 11.8% in each of their past three games (two with Quenton Nelson still on the team), and last week they allowed a 45.9% pass rush pressure rate against Jacksonville, their second-worst rate on the season. Mind you, that's in a game the Jaguars lost their best D-tackle and one of their best pass rushers in. Daniel Jones has faced bad defenses this season and he's come away looking rough. Jones' efficiency has nosedived, and his gun-shy nature has limited the Colts' pass game all year. I'm not convinced Jones will take advantage of this cake matchup, leaving Tyler Warren, Keenan Allen and Josh Downs to get by on volume. Kansas City's pass rush has been noticeably quiet (nine sacks and a 3.6% sack rate this year), and Geno Smith's splits are noticeably better when he's not pressured -- his past two games are recent examples. And if that's not bad enough, the Chiefs figure to be down their top two cornerbacks again. Who benefits with Garrett Wilson not expected to play? Adonai Mitchell enters the week 15th among all qualifying wide receivers in target per route run rate (25.7%), so he's got a great shot to lead the Jets in targets even though he's far more of a downfield weapon than short-area target. Omar Cooper Jr. would also be expected to handle plenty of snaps, even after last week's donut. He got open plenty, but Smith kept firing to Wilson and Mitchell. Cooper Jr. has played more snaps in two-tight end formations over the last three weeks than any Jets receiver other than Wilson. He also can fit in nicely as a short-area threat like Wilson had been on 70% of his targets. Mitchell and Cooper are the best options on the Jets to flex.  
Updated: The Jets coaching staff made it clear that Breece Hall will be their starter in his first game back from injury. Is that a peek inside their minds on how they'll use him and Braelon Allen? Keep in mind, it's Allen who for the past four games has been top five among qualifying RBs in yards per rush (5.6), rush EPA, success rate, yards after contact per rush (4.15), explosive rush rate (15.2% of his runs have gone at least 12 yards). You'd think they'd keep leaning on Allen, but it's hard to trust this coaching staff to do anything right, plus it's worth pointing out that Hall had roughly a 60/40 snap share split with Allen in Weeks 1 and 2 before Hall got hurt in Week 3 (Hall played more inside the five-yard line in those games). The uncertainty is a problem, especially since the Chiefs have allowed a running back to land at least 18.5 PPR points three times in their past four games, and every single RB with at least 15 touches against Kansas City has at least 14.5 PPR points thanks to work in the passing game. I started the week expecting Allen to have the better end of a 60/40 split, but maybe the edge should go to Hall since he had 10 receptions on 10 targes through Week 3 compared to four receptions on five targets for Allen in those same games. MUST-START: Kenneth Walker IIISTART: Patrick Mahomes, Rashee Rice, Travis KelceFLEX: Adonai Mitchell, Breece Hall, Braelon Allen, Omar Cooper Jr. (low-end PPR flex)SIT: Geno Smith (bye-week QB), Xavier Worthy, Mason Taylor, Emmett Johnson, Chiefs DST, Jets DST

                10.0-7.00
            
        
        
            
                6.99 - 5.01
            
        
        
            
                5.00 - 0
            
        
                    
                Sit 'em
            
            
Jameson Williams has drawn the attention of Jared Goff to the point where the speedy receiver is not only seeing increased targets ahead of Sam LaPorta, but also taking a small share of targets away from Amon-Ra St. Brown! Coming out of the bye, it was Goff who found Williams as a second read on five of his nine targets, including his second touchdown (and on an end-zone target later in the game). That led to at least half of Williams' six targets in Week 8 being throws designed for him, including the deep post shot he gained 46 yards on. This is great for Detroit's offense, but a little depressing for those who start LaPorta and, to a lesser degree, St. Brown. Dolphins coach Jeff Hafley has plenty of experience scheming against Detroit's personnel from his days in Green Bay, but his current group of defenders doesn't blitz much, doesn't pressure the quarterback enough, ranks league average in PPR points allowed to wide receivers in their past three, and ranks third-worst in PPR points allowed to tight ends on the season. The 49ers pass rush should be the best its been in maybe two years with Nick Bosa coming back from injury and DeForest Buckner rejoining the team after getting traded out of Indianapolis. Without them the Niners had been solid at getting to the quarterback, save for their Week 7 loss at Atlanta when Michael Penix Jr. got the ball out quickly. Kirk Cousins sports a season-long 2.7 time-to-throw average, which is fairly quick, but just 32.5% of his pass attempts have gone out under 2.5 seconds and the results on those throws are pretty mixed (league-high 6.2-yard average throw depth, but third-worst completion rate and just three touchdowns). It's the pass rush pressure that makes me nervous -- like many quarterbacks, Cousins is decidedly worse when pressured (much lower completion rate, fewer yards per attempt, and a TD rate cut by more than half), and if he's going to hold the ball even a decent percentage of the time against this revamped 49ers pass rush then he could be in trouble. Cousins has also been a garbage-time Fantasy king this season, but if the game's a one-sided blowout then we might see Fernando Mendoza get in the game. It's also worth mentioning that the 49ers lead the NFL in completion rate allowed (37.7%) and top-five in defensive EPA per pass when defending throws of 10-plus air yards. That figures to hurt Tre Tucker's chances of making a big splash.  Could we have seen the Raiders running back switch coming? Perhaps -- Ashton Jeanty was so inefficient as a runner entering last week (3.1 yards per carry, 0.49 yards before contact per rush, 2.8% explosive rush rate) while Mike Washington Jr. had been better (4.9 yards per rush, 1.45 yards before contact per rush, 12.5% explosive rush rate). But the Raiders had seemed hesitant to give Washington a lot of work since his season-high in carries before Week 8 was nine. Game script certainly helped Washington get a lot of work, and while his efficiency waned overall, his rushing average was 4.2 if you eliminated touches inside the five-yard line. Most importantly, Washington gave the Raiders a rushing presence they had not experienced since Week 2 with Jeanty. The worry this week is that the 49ers crush the Raiders defense and forces Las Vegas into a pass-heavy game script. That could work out for Brock Bowers and maybe also Michael Mayer, but that would seemingly benefit Jeanty since he remains effective -- and used -- in passing situations. Jeanty ran more than twice as many routes as Washington last week.
